title: Spiritual eyes, ears, and hands
source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ὡς ἐν τόπῳ ὄντος τοῦ θεοῦ πευσόμεθά τινος καὶ ἐροῦμεν· πῶς ἴωμεν πρὸς αὐτόν; κρείττων γὰρ ὁ θεὸς παντὸς τόπου καὶ περιεκτικὸς παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν, καὶ οὐδέν ἐστι τὸ περιέχον τὸν θεόν. τὸ ἰέναι οὖν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν οὐ σωματικῶς προστέτακται ἡμῖν, τὸ „ὀπίσω κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ σου πορεύσῃ,“ οὐδὲ σωματικῶς ὁ προφήτης κολληθεὶς τῷ θεῷ φησιν ἐν τῇ εὐχῇ· „ἐκολλήθη ὀπίσω σου ἡ ψυχή μου.“ καταψεύδεται οὖν ἡμῶν Κέλσος λέγων προσδέχεσθαι ἡμᾶς ὀφθαλμοῖς σώματος θεὸν ὄψεσθαι καὶ ὠσὶ τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούεσθαι καὶ χερσὶν αἰσθηταῖς ψαύειν αὐτοῦ. οἴδαμεν δὲ ὁμωνύμως τοῖς σώματος ὀφθαλμοῖς λεγομένους ὑπὸ τῶν θείων λόγων ὀφθαλμοὺς, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τὰ ὦτα καὶ τὰς χεῖρας καὶ τὸ τούτων παραδοξότερον, αἴσθησιν θειοτέραν καὶ ἑτεροίαν παρὰ τὴν συνήθως ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν ὀνομαζομένην. ἐπὰν γὰρ λέγῃ ὁ προφήτης· „ἀποκάλυψον τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου, καὶ κατανοήσω τὰ θαυμάσιά σου ἐκ τοῦ νόμου (σου“ ἤ·) „ἡ ἐντολὴ κυρίου τηλαυγὴς, φωτίζουσα ὀφθαλμοὺς,“ ἤ· „φώτισον τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου, μή ποτε ὑπνώσω εἰς θάνατον,“ οὐχ οὕτως τις ἐμβρόντητός ἐστιν, ὡς νομίζειν ὀφθαλμοῖς σώματος κατανοεῖσθαι „τὰ θαυμάσια“ τοῦ θείου „νόμου,“ ἢ τὴν τοῦ κυρίου ἐντολὴν φωτιστικὴν εἶναι τῶν τοῦ σώματος ὀφθαλμῶν, ἢ ὕπνον θανάτου ἐποιστικὸν συμβαίνειν περὶ τοὺς τοῦ σώματος ὀφθαλμούς. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὰν λέγῃ ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν· „ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω,“ καὶ ὁ τυχὼν συνίησι περὶ θειοτέρων ταῦτα λέγεσθαι ὤτων, κἂν λέγηται „λόγος κυρίου“ γεγονέναι ἐν χειρὶ Ἱερεμίου τοῦ προφήτου ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς, ἢ νόμος „ἐν χειρὶ“ Μωϋσέως, ἢ ὅτι „ταῖς χερσί μου ἐζήτησα τὸν θεὸν καὶ οὐκ ἠπατήθην,“ οὐχ οὕτως ἐστί τις ἀνόητος, ὡς μὴ ἐκλαμβάνειν χεῖράς τινας εἶναι τροπικῶς καλουμένας, περὶ ὧν καὶ Ἰωάννης λέγει· „αἱ χεῖρες ἡμῶν ἐψηλάφησαν περὶ τοῦ λόγου τῆς ζωῆς,“ εἰ δὲ καὶ περὶ τῆς κρείττονος αἰσθήσεως καὶ οὐ σωματικῆς βούλει ἀπὸ τῶν ἱερῶν γραμμάτων μαθεῖν, ἄκουσον Σολομῶντος ἐν ταῖς Παροιμίαις λέγοντος· „αἴσθησιν θείαν εὑρήσεις.“
pass_a_gloss: But neither, as God being in a place (τόπος), shall we inquire (πυνθάνομαι) of anyone and say: ‘how may we go to him?’ For God is greater (κρείττων) than every place and encompassing (περιεκτικός) of everything whatever, and nothing is the encompassing (περιέχον) God. The going (ἰέναι) then to God is not bodily (σωματικῶς) commanded (προστάσσω) us, the ‘after (ὀπίσω) the Lord your God you shall walk (πορεύομαι)’, nor bodily does the prophet, joined (κολλάομαι) to God, say in the prayer (εὐχή): ‘my soul (ψυχή) was joined after you.’ Celsus then lies against (καταψεύδομαι) us, saying that we expect (προσδέχομαι) to see God with eyes of the body and with ears to hear his voice (φωνή) and with sensible (αἰσθηταί) hands to touch (ψαύω) him. But we know eyes spoken of by the divine words homonymously (ὁμωνύμως) with the eyes of the body, likewise also the ears and the hands, and what is more paradoxical (παραδοξότερον) than these, a more divine (θειοτέρα) and different-in-kind (ἑτεροία) sense (αἴσθησις) beside the one customarily (συνήθως) named by the many. For whenever the prophet says ‘uncover (ἀποκαλύπτω) my eyes, and I will consider your wonders (θαυμάσια) from (ἐκ) your law (νόμος)’ or ‘the commandment (ἐντολή) of the Lord far-shining (τηλαυγής), enlightening (φωτίζω) eyes’ or ‘enlighten my eyes, lest ever I sleep (ὑπνόω) into death’, no one is so thunderstruck (ἐμβρόντητος) as to think that the wonders of the divine law are perceived with eyes of the body, or the Lord’s commandment illuminative (φωτιστική) of the eyes of the body, or that sleep bringing on (ἐποιστικός) death occurs about the eyes of the body. But also whenever our Saviour (σωτήρ) says ‘he who has ears to hear, let him hear’, even the chance person (ὁ τυχών) understands (συνίημι) these to be said about more divine ears; and even if the ‘word (λόγος) of the Lord’ is said to have come in the hand (ἐν χειρί) of Jeremiah the prophet or someone else, or law ‘in the hand’ of Moses, or that ‘with my hands I sought (ζητέω) God and was not deceived (ἀπατάω)’, no one is so senseless (ἀνόητος) as not to take (ἐκλαμβάνω) certain hands to be figuratively (τροπικῶς) called, about which John also says: ‘our hands handled (ψηλαφάω) about the Word of life (λόγος τῆς ζωῆς)’. And if you wish to learn also about the better and not bodily sense from the sacred writings, hear Solomon in the Proverbs (Παροιμίαι) saying: ‘a divine sense (αἴσθησις θεία) you will find.’
pass_b_english: But neither shall we ask anyone, as though God were in a place, and say: “How are we to go to him?” For God is greater than every place and contains all things whatever, and there is nothing that contains God. So the command given us, “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 13:4), does not tell us to go to God in a bodily way; nor is it in a bodily way that the prophet, who clung to God, says in his prayer: “My soul has clung close after you” (Psalm 63:8).

Celsus, then, lies about us when he says that we expect to see God with the eyes of the body, to hear his voice with our ears, and to touch him with hands perceptible to the senses. But we know that the divine words speak of eyes that bear the same name as the eyes of the body, and likewise of ears and of hands, and, what is more surprising still, of a sense more divine than, and different in kind from, the one that most people ordinarily call by that name.

For when the prophet says, “Uncover my eyes, and I will consider your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18), or, “The commandment of the Lord shines far, giving light to the eyes” (Psalm 19:8), or, “Give light to my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Psalm 13:3), no one is so dull-witted as to think that “the wonders” of the divine “law” are perceived with the eyes of the body, or that the Lord’s commandment gives light to the eyes of the body, or that the sleep that brings on death befalls the eyes of the body.

Again, when our Saviour says, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8), even an ordinary person understands that this is said of more divine ears. And when it is said that “the word of the Lord” came “by the hand” of Jeremiah the prophet (Jeremiah 37:2), or of someone else (Haggai 1:1), or that the law came “by the hand” of Moses (Leviticus 26:46), or, “With my hands I sought God, and I was not deceived” (Psalm 77:2), no one is so foolish as not to take it that there are hands so called in a figurative sense. Of these John too says: “Our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1).
And if you wish to learn from the sacred writings about the better sense as well, the one that is not bodily, hear Solomon saying in Proverbs: “You will find a divine sense” (Proverbs 2:5).

choices.choice: The opening question repeats the Christians’ question as Celsus framed it in chapter 33; it is in double marks as a quoted question. Celsus’s charge (‘we expect to see God with the eyes of the body…’) is indirect report, so no quotation marks. LXX Psalm numbers converted: 62:9 → 63:8; 118:18 → 119:18; 18:9 → 19:8; 12:4 → 13:3; 76:3 → 77:2. Psalm 118:18 LXX reads ‘your wonders out of your law’ (τὰ θαυμάσιά σου ἐκ τοῦ νόμου σου); translated so in the quotation, while Origen’s own comment says ‘the wonders of the divine law’. ‘You shall walk after the Lord your God’: Deuteronomy 13:4 (LXX/Hebrew 13:5) has the plural ‘you shall walk’; Origen gives the singular; the identification is probable, not certain. κολληθείς and ἐκολλήθη are the same verb, so ‘clung … clung’ keeps Origen’s link. ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear’ with ἀκούειν matches Luke 8:8 exactly (also Luke 14:35; Mark 4:9 and Matthew 11:15 are close forms). ‘The word of the Lord … by the hand of Jeremiah’: no single verse matches exactly; Jeremiah 37:2 (LXX 44:2, ‘the words of the Lord which he spoke by the hand of Jeremiah the prophet’) is the nearest, and Haggai 1:1 (‘the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet’) is the exact formula for ‘someone else’. ‘The law by the hand of Moses’ is a recurring formula; Leviticus 26:46 cited as a representative instance (compare Numbers 36:13). Psalm 77:2 LXX: ‘with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived’; Origen compresses it. 1 John 1:1 ‘the Word of life’ is capitalised as referring to Christ. ‘You will find a divine sense’ is Origen’s regular form of Proverbs 2:5; the standard LXX reads ‘knowledge of God (ἐπίγνωσιν θεοῦ) you will find’; Origen’s wording is translated as he gives it. Koetschau’s supplement (σου ἤ) in the Psalm 119:18 quotation is accepted. ἐμβρόντητος (lit. thunderstruck) means stupefied, stupid; rendered ‘dull-witted’.
Citation corrected: ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear’ (with ἀκούειν) is Luke 8:8 exactly; Matthew 11:15 lacks ‘to hear’ in the Greek
Added Haggai 1:1 beside ‘or of someone else’: it carries the exact formula ‘the word of the Lord came by the hand of … the prophet’
Psalm 119:18 quotation brought to the LXX wording Origen gives: ‘your wonders out of your law’
‘the prophet, who was joined to God’ to ‘who clung to God’, keeping Origen’s word link with ‘My soul has clung’
‘so dazed’ (weak for ἐμβρόντητος, which means stupid here) to ‘so dull-witted’; ‘hands that the senses perceive’ to ‘hands perceptible to the senses’
Restored omitted particles: ‘But neither’ (ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿), ‘But we know’ (δέ), and ‘as well’ for καί in the Proverbs sentence
Title ‘Eyes, Ears, and Hands of the Spirit’ could be read as the Holy Spirit; changed to ‘Spiritual Eyes, Ears, and Hands’
Deuteronomy 13:4, Psalms 63:8, 19:8, 13:3, 77:2 (LXX numbers converted), Leviticus 26:46, 1 John 1:1, Proverbs 2:5 checked

choices.issue: open doubt for the owner (not a blocker)
choices.choice: 7.34: no single verse matches 'the word of the Lord came by the hand of Jeremiah' exactly. Jeremiah 37:2 (LXX 44:2) is the nearest, and the uncertainty is noted. Deuteronomy 13:4 for the singular 'you shall walk after the Lord your God' is likely but not certain.
